title: Anne and Joachim
hookLine: tradition names Mary's parents; their feast is kept on 26 July
last: NO ONE IS UNCLEAN TO GOD.

lines: SOMEBODY TAUGHT YOU TO TIE YOUR SHOES.
cards: Somebody taught you to tie your shoes. Somebody sat up with you through a fever. People like that are easy to forget, because they were simply always there.
Mary had people like that: a mother and a father who carried her, fed her, and taught her to pray. Here's the honest part: the Bible never names them. Not once.
The Gospels open with Mary already a young woman. The names Catholics use come from an early story told outside the Bible.

teach.h: AN OLD STORY, OUTSIDE THE BIBLE.
teach.b: The story comes from an early Christian writing called the Protoevangelium of James. It's not in the Bible, and the Church has never treated it as Scripture, but its names and some of its scenes stuck.
Joachim is a good, generous man, but he and his wife Anne have no children, and at the temple he's shamed for it. So he goes out into the wilderness to fast and pray for forty days.

At home, Anne sits in her garden and grieves. She looks up into a tree, sees a nest of baby birds, and weeps: even the birds have little ones. Then an angel comes to each of them, separately: you will have a child.

Joachim hurries home, Anne runs to meet him at the city gate, and they embrace. Painters have come back to that moment again and again. Their daughter is Mary, and Anne, the story says, dedicates her to God.
Anne is the English form of the Hebrew Hannah, meaning grace or favor, the name of the prophet Samuel's mother, who also prayed for a child for years.
Catholics keep their feast together on July twenty-sixth, and as Jesus's grandparents, they're the patron saints of grandparents.
Pope Francis even set aside a day in July for grandparents and older people, near their feast.
Catholics read it as more than a sweet story: grace arriving through an ordinary family, slowly, through people who raised someone and are mostly forgotten.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Joachim and Anne on 26 July, pray to them as patrons of grandparents, and many churches and shrines, like Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré in Quebec, are named for Anne.

games.q: you're Joachim. you've been shamed at the temple because you have no children. what do you do?
o: go into the wilderness to fast and pray.
games.why: in the old story he fasts and prays for forty days, and an angel tells him and Anne, separately, they'll have a child.

practice: Let a face come to mind, a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a coach, a neighbor, anyone who helped raise you: not the perfect version, the real one.

Remember one specific thing they did, a meal, a ride, a word, and let yourself be grateful for that one thing. If they've died, you can hold them with love; if you pray, you can thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Hannah. The Hebrew name behind Anne, meaning grace, given to Mary's mother in an old, unbiblical story.

orig.note: Hebrew: Hannah, grace or favor. Anne is its English form.

carryVoice: Your line: someone raised her too. Their names live on in an old story. Seventy-eight days and counting.

sources.ref: Pope Francis, Angelus of 31 January 2021 (World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly)
